transcript.heading: News Report One (American Male)
paras: A new study has found that spending time in nature—even just two hours a week—can significantly improve mental health and well-being, according to researchers at the University of Exeter. The study surveyed over 20,000 people and found that those who spent at least two hours a week in natural settings like parks, forests, or beaches reported significantly better mental health and higher life satisfaction than those who spent less time in nature. The benefits were seen across all age groups, income levels, and both men and women. Researchers say that being in nature reduces stress, lowers blood pressure, and improves mood. They note that you don't have to go to a remote wilderness area to get benefits—even a local park or green space can make a difference.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Female)
paras: The city of Seattle has become the latest major US city to ban single-use plastic straws and utensils in restaurants and food service businesses, as part of its efforts to reduce plastic pollution and protect the environment. The ban applies to all restaurants, cafes, food trucks, and other food service establishments, which can no longer provide plastic straws, forks, knives, and spoons unless a customer specifically requests them. Instead, businesses are encouraged to use compostable or reusable alternatives. Supporters say the ban will help reduce the amount of plastic waste that ends up in landfills and oceans. Critics argue that the ban is inconvenient and that alternative products are more expensive. But city officials say the ban is an important step toward reducing plastic pollution and protecting marine life.

paras: Researchers at Stanford University have developed a new type of flexible, wearable battery that can be stretched, bent, and even washed without losing its ability to hold a charge. Unlike traditional batteries, which are rigid and bulky, this new battery is thin, lightweight, and flexible, making it ideal for use in wearable technology like smart watches, fitness trackers, and even smart clothing. The battery uses a special type of polymer electrolyte that's both flexible and safe, and it can be recharged hundreds of times. Researchers say that this type of flexible battery could enable a new generation of wearable devices that are more comfortable and more durable than current devices. The technology is still in the development stage, but researchers are working to improve its energy density and bring it to market.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Jessica): Hey Ryan, how's the new job going? You've been there for about a month now, right?
Man (Ryan): Hmm... it's okay, I guess. To be honest, I'm not really enjoying it as much as I thought I would.
Woman: Oh no, that's too bad. What's wrong? I thought you were excited about this marketing job.

Man: I was excited! But now that I'm actually doing it, it's just... not what I expected. The work is kind of boring, and I feel like I'm not really learning anything new. And the hours are long—way longer than I thought they would be.
Woman: Yeah, that sounds tough. What kind of work are you doing? I thought marketing would be creative and interesting.

Man: Well, I thought so too. But most of my job is just data entry and making spreadsheets. I barely get to do any creative work. And my boss is really micromanaging—she checks every little thing I do and it feels like she doesn't trust me.
Woman: That sounds frustrating. What about the people you work with? Are they nice?
Man: The people are nice enough, I guess. But everyone is so busy and stressed out all the time. There's not much of a team atmosphere. And I feel like I'm just a number, not a person.
Woman: Hmm. Have you talked to your boss about any of this? Maybe you could ask for more interesting projects or more responsibility.
Man: I don't know... I don't want to seem like I'm complaining. And I'm still new, so I feel like I should just do what I'm told and prove myself first.

Woman: Yeah, I get that. But if you're unhappy, you should probably say something. Otherwise, things might not change. What about work-life balance? You said the hours are long—are you working a lot of overtime?

Man: Yeah, pretty much. I'm usually at the office from 8 am to 7 or 8 pm, and I often have to work on weekends too. I barely have time for anything else. I used to love playing guitar and going to the gym, but I haven't done either in weeks.
Woman: Wow, that's a lot. That doesn't sound sustainable. You're going to burn out if you keep working like that.
Man: Yeah, I know. I'm already feeling pretty burnt out. And the worst part is, I'm not even sure if I want to stay in marketing. Maybe I made the wrong career choice.
Woman: Hmm, that's a big question. What did you do before this job?
Man: Before this, I worked at a non-profit doing communications. It paid less, but I felt like the work was meaningful. And I had better work-life balance.
Woman: Oh, so you liked that job better? Why did you leave?
Man: I thought I wanted to advance my career and make more money. And everyone told me that marketing was a good field with lots of opportunities. But now I'm not so sure.
Woman: Well, it's only been a month. Maybe you should give it more time. You're still learning the job and the company. It might get better.
Man: Yeah, you're probably right. I don't want to make a hasty decision. But I also don't want to stay somewhere that makes me miserable.

Woman: Of course not. Why don't you give it another month or two, and see if things improve? In the meantime, maybe you can start thinking about what you really want. What's important to you in a job?
Man: That's a good question. I guess I want work that's meaningful and interesting. And I want to have a life outside of work too. I don't want my job to be my whole identity.
Woman: Those are all reasonable things to want. You don't have to choose between a good career and a good life.
Man: Yeah, you're right. Thanks for listening, Jessica. It helps to talk about it.
Woman: No problem. Let me know how it goes, okay? And if you ever want to talk more, I'm here.
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Male + British Female)
paras: Man (Liam): Hey Emma, can I talk to you about something? I'm having trouble with my history paper and I need some advice.
Woman (Emma): Sure, Liam! What's going on? What's the paper about?
Man: It's about the Industrial Revolution. We have to write about one aspect of it, and I'm having trouble deciding what to focus on. There's so much to write about—I don't know where to start.
Woman: Oh, the Industrial Revolution is such a big topic. That makes sense that you're feeling overwhelmed. What are you interested in?

Man: I'm not sure. I've been reading about the environmental impact of the Industrial Revolution, and that seems interesting. But I also think the social changes are fascinating—like how people's lives changed when they moved from farms to factories.
Woman: Both of those are great topics. Which one are you more passionate about?

Man: Hmm, I think the environmental impact is more interesting to me. I feel like it's relevant to what's happening today with climate change. But I'm worried there might not be enough information about it, or that it's too broad.

Woman: No, that's a great topic! And it's definitely not too broad—you just need to narrow it down. What specifically about the environmental impact interests you? Air pollution? Water pollution? Deforestation?

Man: I've been reading about air pollution in industrial cities like Manchester and Birmingham. It's crazy how bad it was—like, the sky was black all the time from all the coal smoke. And people got really sick from it.

Woman: Yeah, that's a really interesting topic. And you're right—it's very relevant to today. You could talk about how the Industrial Revolution was the beginning of the large-scale air pollution and carbon emissions that we're still dealing with today.
Man: That's exactly what I was thinking! But I'm not sure how to structure the paper. Do you have any tips?
Woman: Well, first you need a clear thesis statement—what's your main argument? What are you trying to prove?

Man: Hmm, I guess my main argument would be that the Industrial Revolution had a huge and lasting environmental impact, especially on air quality, and that many of the environmental problems we face today have their roots in that period.
Woman: That's a strong thesis! Good. Now, what points are you going to use to support that argument?

Man: Well, I could talk about coal use and air pollution in industrial cities. I could talk about the health effects on people who lived there. And I could talk about how the Industrial Revolution set the stage for modern climate change.

Woman: Perfect. Those are three solid points. You could structure your paper with an introduction that states your thesis, then three body paragraphs each covering one of those points, and then a conclusion that wraps it up and connects it to today.
Man: That makes sense. What about sources? Where should I look for information?

Woman: Well, start with the textbook and the readings from class. Then you can use the library's databases to find academic articles and books. Make sure you use reliable sources—no random websites. And don't forget to cite everything properly.
Man: Yeah, I know. Citations are always the worst part. What about the length? The paper has to be 10 pages. Do you think I can write 10 pages about this topic?
Woman: Definitely. If you do enough research, you'll have more than enough information. Just make sure each body paragraph is well developed with examples and evidence to support your points.
Man: Okay, that's reassuring. What about the introduction? I always have trouble writing introductions.

Woman: Oh, I know what you mean. I usually write the introduction last, after I've written the rest of the paper. That way I know exactly what I'm introducing. Start with something interesting to hook the reader—maybe a vivid description of what industrial cities were like, or a surprising fact. Then give some background and end with your thesis statement.
Man: That's a good tip. I'll try that. Thanks so much for your help, Emma. I feel a lot less overwhelmed now.
Woman: No problem! I'm happy to help. And if you want, you can send me a draft when you're done and I can look it over for you.
Man: Really? That would be amazing! Thank you so much.
Woman: Of course. Good luck with it! I'm sure it'll be great.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Female)
paras: The Great Wall of China is one of the most famous and impressive structures in the world, and it's often called the longest man-made structure ever built. But there are many myths and misconceptions about the Great Wall, and the real story is even more fascinating than the myths.

First, let's talk about one of the most common myths: that the Great Wall is visible from space with the naked eye. This is a widely believed myth, but it's simply not true. The wall is only about 6 to 7 meters wide, which is too narrow to be visible from space with the naked eye. Astronauts have confirmed that you can't see the Great Wall from the moon, and it's very difficult to see even from low Earth orbit without magnification.

Second, the Great Wall isn't just one single wall—it's actually a series of walls and fortifications that were built over many centuries by different dynasties. The earliest sections of the wall were built over 2,000 years ago, during the Warring States period, to protect different states from each other. Later, during the Qin Dynasty, the first emperor of China connected and extended these walls to create a unified defense system against nomadic invaders from the north.

But the most famous sections of the wall that people visit today were built much later, during the Ming Dynasty, from the 14th to the 17th centuries. The Ming Dynasty built the wall on a massive scale, using bricks and stone instead of the rammed earth that was used in earlier walls. The Ming wall is about 8,850 kilometers long, and it includes watchtowers, barracks, and fortresses.

Another common myth is that the wall was built by forced labor and that millions of people died building it. While it's true that many people worked on the wall and that conditions were often harsh, the idea that millions of people died and were buried in the wall is probably exaggerated.

And how effective was the wall at keeping invaders out? Well, it was partially effective. It worked well for small raids and for controlling trade and immigration. But it couldn't stop major invasions—several times throughout history, invaders were able to get past the wall, either by finding a weak point or by bribing the guards. The wall was most effective as a psychological barrier and as a symbol of Chinese power and unity.

Today, the Great Wall is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of China's most popular tourist attractions. Millions of people visit it every year. But much of the wall is in poor condition, especially in remote areas, and it's being eroded by time and weather. Conservation efforts are underway to protect and restore this amazing historical structure.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Male)
paras: Color psychology is the study of how colors affect our emotions, behavior, and perceptions. While the field is still relatively new and there's much we don't know, research has shown that colors can have a significant impact on how we feel and how we behave.

Different colors are often associated with different emotions and meanings. For example, warm colors like red, orange, and yellow are often associated with energy, warmth, and excitement. Red is a powerful color that can increase heart rate and create a sense of urgency—it's often used in sales and marketing to grab attention and encourage action. Orange is energetic and friendly, and yellow is cheerful and optimistic.

Cool colors like blue, green, and purple, on the other hand, are often associated with calmness, relaxation, and stability. Blue is one of the most popular colors, and it's often associated with trust, reliability, and peace. That's why many banks and tech companies use blue in their branding—it makes people feel secure and confident. Green is associated with nature, health, and growth, and it's often used by environmental and health-related brands. Purple is often associated with creativity, luxury, and spirituality.

But it's important to remember that color associations aren't universal—they can vary a lot depending on culture, personal experience, and context. For example, in Western cultures, white is associated with purity and weddings, but in many Eastern cultures, white is associated with death and mourning. Similarly, red is associated with luck and happiness in China, but in some Western cultures it's associated with danger and warning.

Personal experience also plays a big role in how we perceive colors. If you have positive memories associated with a certain color, you're likely to feel positively about it. And if you have negative memories associated with a color, you might feel negatively about it.

Color psychology is used in many different fields, from marketing and advertising to interior design to therapy. In marketing, colors are carefully chosen to create certain feelings and associations with brands. In interior design, colors are used to create certain moods in different rooms—calming colors for bedrooms, energizing colors for gyms, and so on. In color therapy, different colors are used to treat various physical and mental health conditions, though the scientific evidence for color therapy is limited.

While color psychology is fascinating, it's also important not to overstate its effects. Colors can influence our mood and behavior, but they're just one factor among many. And the effects are often subtle and depend on many different variables. Still, understanding how colors affect us can be useful in many areas of life.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: Urban agriculture—the practice of growing food in cities—is becoming increasingly popular around the world as people look for ways to eat more locally, reduce their environmental impact, and build stronger communities. From small community gardens to large commercial urban farms, urban agriculture takes many forms and offers many benefits.

There are many different types of urban agriculture. Community gardens are plots of land that are gardened collectively by a group of people, often neighbors. Rooftop gardens are gardens built on top of buildings, which can be used to grow food, reduce energy costs, and manage stormwater. Vertical farms are indoor farms that grow food in stacked layers, using artificial light and controlled environments. And backyard gardens are gardens in people's own yards or on their balconies.

One of the main benefits of urban agriculture is that it reduces the environmental impact of food production. Traditional agriculture requires a lot of land, water, and energy, and food has to be transported long distances from farms to cities, which generates greenhouse gas emissions. Urban agriculture reduces transportation emissions because the food is grown locally. It also reduces packaging waste, since locally grown food doesn't need as much packaging. And urban farms and gardens can help reduce the "heat island" effect in cities, where cities are hotter than surrounding rural areas because of all the concrete and asphalt. Plants help cool the air through transpiration.

Another benefit is that urban agriculture can improve access to fresh, healthy food, especially in low-income neighborhoods that don't have easy access to grocery stores with fresh produce. These neighborhoods are often called "food deserts." Community gardens and urban farms can provide fresh fruits and vegetables to people who might not otherwise have access to them.

Urban agriculture also has social and community benefits. Community gardens bring people together and build community. They give people a chance to work together, share knowledge and resources, and get to know their neighbors. Gardening can also be therapeutic and reduce stress, and it gives people a sense of purpose and accomplishment.

And of course, urban agriculture provides educational opportunities. Children and adults alike can learn about where food comes from, how plants grow, and the importance of agriculture and the environment.

Of course, urban agriculture also faces challenges. Space is limited in cities, and finding suitable land can be difficult. Soil quality can be poor, and there can be concerns about contamination from previous land use. Water access can also be a challenge. And zoning laws and regulations sometimes make it difficult to start urban farms or community gardens.

But despite these challenges, urban agriculture is growing and thriving in cities around the world. And as more people become interested in local food, sustainability, and community, it's likely to continue to grow in the future.
